--- title: "Choosing measures that match the objective" description: "Work backwards from the sentence you intend to write. Four models, three objectives, and a threshold chosen from costs rather than from a default." order: 6 categories: [validation, metrics] --- ## The objective hidden in a default Every page in this section has compared models by a number. None of them has asked where the number came from, and the honest answer is usually "it was the default". Defaults encode an objective. RMSE assumes you care about squared error at every station equally. Accuracy assumes the two kinds of mistake cost the same. A 0.5 threshold assumes it even harder. If your actual objective is a stock total, or a shortlist of fifty stations to dive, those defaults will happily rank the models in the wrong order, and this page shows them doing it. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. The R tab is what produced the tables and figures you see; the Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent, shown for translation rather than executed by the site. Figures stay in R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. It is real code, not pseudocode: it runs against the same files through `python/mlbasic_data.py`, and `python/check-snippets.py` executes every snippet in the site to keep it honest. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly**: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## The idea Write the sentence from the discussion section first, then choose the measure that would be false if the sentence were false. | The sentence you want to write | The measure that tests it | | --- | --- | | "We mapped predicted abundance across the shelf" | per-station error: RMSE or MAE | | "Total abundance in the survey area is about *N*" | bias in the sum, not per-station error | | "These fifty stations are where the species is densest" | what a ranked shortlist actually finds | | "Flag a station for follow-up if …" | expected cost at the chosen threshold | | "Abundance peaks at 80 m" | none of the above; see §6 on confounding | The last row is a reminder rather than a recipe. No predictive measure tests whether a relationship is causal, and a model can be excellent at the first four while being wrong about the fifth. ## Worked example: four models, three objectives Same five models as the [regression measures page](regression-metrics.qmd), same folds, same pooled out-of-fold predictions. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() d <- survey |> dplyr::select(abundance, depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3, salinity_psu, substrate, season, longitude, latitude) |> drop_na() formula_env <- abundance ~ poly(depth_m, 2) + poly(temperature_c, 2) + log1p(chlorophyll_mg_m3) + salinity_psu + substrate + season + longitude + latitude fitters <- list( `mean only` = \(tr, te) rep(mean(tr$abundance), nrow(te)), `Poisson GLM` = \(tr, te) predict(glm(formula_env, tr, family = poisson), te, type = "response"), `negative binomial` = \(tr, te) predict(glm.nb(formula_env, tr), te, type = "response"), `log-transformed lm` = \(tr, te) expm1(predict(lm(update(formula_env, log1p(abundance) ~ .), tr), te)), `random forest` = \(tr, te) predict(ranger(abundance ~ ., tr, num.trees = 500, seed = 1), te)$predictions ) set.seed(61) folds <- vfold_cv(d, v = 10) out_of_fold <- imap_dfr(fitters, \(f, name) { map_dfr(folds$splits, \(s) { tr <- analysis(s); te <- assessment(s) tibble(model = name, obs = te$abundance, pred = f(tr, te)) }) }) ``` ::: ## Python ```python import numpy as np import pandas as pd import statsmodels.formula.api as smf from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.model_selection import KFold from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() columns = ["abundance", "depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude"] d = survey[columns].dropna().reset_index(drop=True) # patsy has no poly(), so the squared terms are written out. C() is factor(). formula_env = ("abundance ~ depth_m + I(depth_m**2)" " + temperature_c + I(temperature_c**2)" " + np.log1p(chlorophyll_mg_m3) + salinity_psu" " + C(substrate) + C(season) + longitude + latitude") forest_columns = pd.get_dummies(d.drop(columns="abundance"), drop_first=True) def forest_predict(tr, te): model = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, random_state=1).fit( forest_columns.loc[tr.index], tr["abundance"]) return model.predict(forest_columns.loc[te.index]) fitters = { "mean only": lambda tr, te: np.repeat(tr["abundance"].mean(), len(te)), "Poisson GLM": lambda tr, te: smf.glm( formula_env, tr, family=sm.families.Poisson()).fit().predict(te), # negativebinomial() estimates the dispersion with the coefficients, as # MASS::glm.nb() does; statsmodels' GLM family wants it fixed in advance. "negative binomial": lambda tr, te: smf.negativebinomial( formula_env, tr).fit(method="bfgs", maxiter=2000, disp=0).predict(te), "log-transformed lm": lambda tr, te: np.expm1( smf.ols(formula_env.replace("abundance ~", "np.log1p(abundance) ~"), tr) .fit().predict(te)), "random forest": forest_predict, } import statsmodels.api as sm folds = KFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=61) out_of_fold = pd.concat([ pd.DataFrame({"model": name, "fold": i, "obs": d.iloc[held]["abundance"].to_numpy(), "pred": np.asarray(fit(d.iloc[rows], d.iloc[held]))}) for name, fit in fitters.items() for i, (rows, held) in enumerate(folds.split(d), start=1) ], ignore_index=True) len(out_of_fold) ``` ::: The third objective needs a definition. Suppose the ship can revisit fifty stations. We send it to the fifty the model ranks highest, and count how many individuals are actually there. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} budget <- 50 observed <- filter(out_of_fold, model == "mean only")$obs perfect <- sum(sort(observed, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(budget)]) objectives <- out_of_fold |> summarise( `mapping: RMSE` = rmse_vec(obs, pred), `stock total: pred / obs` = sum(pred) / sum(obs), `targeting: caught in 50` = sum(obs[order(pred, decreasing = TRUE)][seq_len(budget)]), .by = model) |> mutate(`share of a perfect shortlist` = `targeting: caught in 50` / perfect) objectives |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | mapping: RMSE| stock total: pred / obs| targeting: caught in 50| share of a perfect shortlist| |:------------------|-------------:|-----------------------:|-----------------------:|----------------------------:| |mean only | 4.826| 1.000| 183| 0.215| |Poisson GLM | 4.216| 1.002| 499| 0.586| |negative binomial | 4.215| 0.998| 499| 0.586| |log-transformed lm | 4.461| 0.694| 481| 0.565| |random forest | 4.363| 1.034| 456| 0.536|
::: ::: ## Python ```python from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error budget = 50 observed = out_of_fold.loc[out_of_fold["model"] == "mean only", "obs"].to_numpy() perfect = np.sort(observed)[::-1][:budget].sum() def objective(group): shortlist = group.sort_values("pred", ascending=False).head(budget) return pd.Series({ "mapping: RMSE": root_mean_squared_error(group["obs"], group["pred"]), "stock total: pred / obs": group["pred"].sum() / group["obs"].sum(), "targeting: caught in 50": shortlist["obs"].sum(), }) objectives = out_of_fold.groupby("model", sort=False).apply( objective, include_groups=False).reset_index() objectives["share of a perfect shortlist"] = ( objectives["targeting: caught in 50"] / perfect) objectives.round(3) ``` ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c(`individuals in the whole survey` = sum(observed), `a perfect shortlist of 50 finds` = perfect, `50 stations chosen at random find` = budget * mean(observed)) |> round(0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> individuals in the whole survey a perfect shortlist of 50 finds #> 2845 851 #> 50 stations chosen at random find #> 198 ``` ::: ::: ## Python ```python pd.Series({ "individuals in the whole survey": observed.sum(), "a perfect shortlist of 50 finds": perfect, "50 stations chosen at random find": budget * observed.mean(), }).round(0) ``` ::: ## Reading down each column Three objectives, and the table reads differently down each column. **The mean-only model is perfect at estimating the total.** Its predicted total is exactly the observed total, ratio 1.000, because that is what a mean is. It has no skill whatsoever: it gives the same answer at every station, has the worst RMSE in the table, and a shortlist built from its rankings finds 183 individuals, essentially what fifty stations picked at random would find. **A measure that checks only an aggregate can be satisfied by a model with no information in it.** If you report a total, report a per-station error beside it. **The ranking objective reverses two models.** The random forest beats the log-transformed linear model on RMSE, 4.363 to 4.461. Send the ship out on their rankings and the log model's fifty stations hold 481 individuals against the forest's 456, which is 5% more, from the model with the worse RMSE. Squared error punished the log model for its low predictions; the shortlist does not care what numbers it printed, only what order it put the stations in. **And no model is close to perfect.** The best shortlist here finds 499 of the 851 individuals a clairvoyant ranking would find, or 59%. That is the honest sentence for a survey plan: not "our model has R² 0.24", which means nothing to a ship's officer, but *"targeting the fifty stations this model ranks highest should find roughly two and a half times as many individuals as fifty stations chosen at random, and about three-fifths of the theoretical maximum."* ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## The shortlist measure is not R² in disguise R² and RMSE are computed from the *values* the model predicts; the shortlist depends only on their *order*. Any monotone transformation of the predictions, halving them all or taking their square root, leaves the shortlist identical and changes RMSE completely. That is exactly the independence you want when the decision is "which stations", not "how many at each". It works the other way too. A model can order stations perfectly and be badly biased, which is why the log-transformed model does well here and disastrously on the total. ::: ## Worked example: a threshold from costs The [classification page](classification-metrics.qmd) showed that accuracy, F1, MCC and Youden's J each want a different cut-off. None of them is the right one, because none of them knows what a mistake costs you. Suppose the decision is whether to send a dive team to confirm presence. A **wasted dive**, a station flagged where nothing is there, costs ship time. A **missed station** costs a gap in the record. Let their relative cost be $k$ dives per missed station, and compute the expected cost per station across all thresholds. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} presence <- survey |> select(present, depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3, salinity_psu, substrate, season, longitude, latitude) |> drop_na() rec <- recipe(present ~ ., data = presence) |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) set.seed(71) presence_folds <- vfold_cv(presence, v = 10, strata = present) probabilities <- map_dfr(presence_folds$splits, \(s) { fitted <- fit(workflow() |> add_recipe(rec) |> add_model(logistic_reg()), analysis(s)) held <- assessment(s) tibble(truth = held$present, .pred_yes = predict(fitted, held, type = "prob")$.pred_yes) }) expected_cost <- function(threshold, k) { flagged <- probabilities$.pred_yes >= threshold missed <- sum(!flagged & probabilities$truth == "yes") wasted <- sum( flagged & probabilities$truth == "no") (missed + k * wasted) / nrow(probabilities) } cost_curves <- expand_grid(k = c(1, 3, 10, 30), cut_off = seq(0.01, 0.99, by = 0.005)) |> mutate(cost = map2_dbl(cut_off, k, expected_cost)) cost_table <- cost_curves |> summarise(`cheapest threshold` = cut_off[which.min(cost)], `cost there` = min(cost), `cost at 0.5` = expected_cost(0.5, first(k)), .by = k) |> mutate(`theory: k/(1+k)` = k / (1 + k), `saved by not using 0.5` = 1 - `cost there` / `cost at 0.5`) |> select(`a wasted dive costs` = k, `cheapest threshold`, `theory: k/(1+k)`, `cost there`, `cost at 0.5`, `saved by not using 0.5`) cost_table |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| a wasted dive costs| cheapest threshold| theory: k/(1+k)| cost there| cost at 0.5| saved by not using 0.5| |-------------------:|------------------:|---------------:|----------:|-----------:|----------------------:| | 1| 0.520| 0.500| 0.207| 0.208| 0.007| | 3| 0.750| 0.750| 0.539| 0.617| 0.126| | 10| 0.965| 0.909| 0.782| 2.046| 0.618| | 30| 0.965| 0.968| 0.782| 6.129| 0.872|
::: ::: ## Python ```python from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_val_predict from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler presence_columns = ["present", "depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude"] presence = pd.get_dummies(survey[presence_columns].dropna(), columns=["substrate", "season"], drop_first=True) X = presence.drop(columns="present") truth = presence["present"].astype(str).to_numpy() model = Pipeline([("normalise", StandardScaler()), ("model", LogisticRegression(C=np.inf, max_iter=2000))]) probabilities = cross_val_predict( model, X, truth, cv=StratifiedKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=71), method="predict_proba")[:, list(np.unique(truth)).index("yes")] def expected_cost(threshold, k): flagged = probabilities >= threshold missed = np.sum(~flagged & (truth == "yes")) wasted = np.sum(flagged & (truth == "no")) return (missed + k * wasted) / len(truth) cut_offs = np.arange(0.01, 0.99 + 1e-9, 0.005) def cheapest(k): costs = np.array([expected_cost(cut, k) for cut in cut_offs]) best = int(np.argmin(costs)) return { "a wasted dive costs": k, "cheapest threshold": cut_offs[best], "theory: k/(1+k)": k / (1 + k), "cost there": costs[best], "cost at 0.5": expected_cost(0.5, k), "saved by not using 0.5": 1 - costs[best] / expected_cost(0.5, k), } cost_table = pd.DataFrame([cheapest(k) for k in (1, 3, 10, 30)]) cost_table.round(3) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} scaled_curves <- cost_curves |> mutate(relative = cost / min(cost), .by = k) |> mutate(label = paste0("a wasted dive costs ", k, "×")) cost_minima <- slice_min(scaled_curves, relative, by = k, with_ties = FALSE) ggplot(scaled_curves, aes(cut_off, relative, colour = factor(k))) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], linewidth = 0.4) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(data = cost_minima, size = 3) + ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = cost_minima, aes(label = label), size = 3.1, seed = 3, direction = "y", nudge_y = 0.12, min.segment.length = 0.3) + scale_y_log10() + scale_colour_ml() + labs(x = "flag the station if the predicted probability exceeds this", y = "expected cost, relative to that curve's best", title = "Where the cheapest threshold sits depends on what a mistake costs") + theme(legend.position = "none") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Expected cost per station against the decision threshold, for four exchange rates between a wasted dive and a missed station. Each curve is scaled to its own minimum, marked with a dot; the dashed line is 0.5. When both errors cost the same the cheapest threshold is 0.52. As wasted dives get more expensive the minimum slides right, to 0.75 and then 0.965, and the penalty for leaving the threshold at 0.5 grows from under 1% to 87%.](choosing-a-metric_files/figure-html/fig-cost-1.png){#fig-cost fig-alt='Four labelled curves on a shared horizontal axis of decision threshold from 0 to 1, with expected cost relative to each curve\'s own minimum on a logarithmic vertical axis from 1 to about 8, and a dashed vertical line at 0.5. Each curve is flat across the left of the plot, dips to a marked minimum, then climbs. The equal-cost curve is lowest on the left at about 1.05, has its minimum at 0.52 and rises to nearly 4 at the right-hand edge. The three-times curve starts near 1.15, bottoms at 0.75 and rises modestly. The ten-times and thirty-times curves start far higher, at about 2.8 and 7.8, and fall steadily across the middle of the plot and reach their minima together at 0.965, close to the right-hand edge. At the dashed line the four curves sit at roughly 1.0, 1.15, 2.6 and 7.8 times their best values.' width=1400} ::: ::: For a model whose probabilities are calibrated, and [the classification page](classification-metrics.qmd) showed this one roughly is, the cost-minimising threshold is $k/(1+k)$, where $k$ is the cost of a wasted dive in units of a missed station. The table shows the empirical optimum landing on it exactly at $k = 3$ and close at $k = 1$ and $k = 30$. At $k = 10$ the empirical best is 0.965 against a theoretical 0.909, because the cost only changes when a station crosses the threshold, so the curve moves in steps and its floor is broad. The last column is the practical point. At $k = 10$, leaving the threshold at 0.5 costs 2.6 times what the cheapest threshold costs. At $k = 30$ it costs nearly eight times as much. One line of code, and no change to the model at all. ::: {.callout-important} ## Say what you assumed You cannot avoid choosing an exchange rate. Using 0.5 is choosing one: it asserts that a wasted dive and a missed station cost exactly the same, which is almost never true and which nobody writes down. "We flagged stations above 0.75, on the assumption that a wasted dive costs about three times a missed record" is a methods sentence a reviewer can argue with, which is the point. It is also the sentence that lets someone with a different ship budget reuse your model. ::: ## Limits of these measures The shortlist measure here used a budget of fifty, and the ordering of models can change with the budget, since a model good at the extreme top of the ranking may be mediocre at 200. Compute it at the budget you actually have. Costs are rarely constant either. The cost of a missed station is not the same for a protected species as for a common one, and the cost of a wasted dive depends on where it is. The framework still works; the single number $k$ becomes a cost per station, and the threshold becomes a per-station threshold. And none of this touches the biggest risk. Every measure in this section scores predictions against observations. If the observations are biased by gear selectivity, observer effects or survey effort that follows ports, then a model that reproduces them perfectly reproduces the bias too, and no validation scheme will tell you. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Key points - Choose the measure from the sentence you intend to write, before you fit anything. - An aggregate-only check is not a validation: the mean-only model estimated the survey total exactly and had no skill at all. - Rankings and values are different objectives. The log-transformed model lost on RMSE and won the fifty-station shortlist, 481 individuals against the forest's 456. - Report decision-shaped numbers: "two and a half times a random shortlist, three-fifths of the theoretical maximum" travels further than "R² 0.24". - The cost-minimising threshold is $k/(1+k)$ for calibrated probabilities. Leaving it at 0.5 cost up to eight times more here than choosing it. - Say what exchange rate you assumed. Using the default is assuming 1:1 silently. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Recompute the shortlist column for budgets of 20, 50, 100 and 200. Does the same model win at every budget? 2. Take the cost framework to the rare-species response from [section 6](../06-assumptions-limitations/class-imbalance.qmd) and find the threshold for *k* = 0.1, a missed detection costing ten wasted dives. How many stations does that flag?
